newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Disinflation seen creating more Yugoslav gloom.
newsitem.headline: Disinflation seen creating more Yugoslav gloom.

text.p: Yugoslavia, plagued in the early 1990s by hyperinflation, may be heading for falling prices, something economists fear could bring the economy to a halt.

Politicians have welcomed the prospect of disinflation but economists said on Tuesday that while this would be desirable for other economies, they favoured a tolerable level of inflation as a stimulus.

"In order to have real deflation, the government would need to go for an even tougher monetary restraint which would put brakes on the entire industry and economy," Pavle Petrovic, leading economist of the private CES-Mecon economic research institute, told Reuters.
Yugoslav statistics showed 0.2 percent month-on-month inflation in May and a 21.3 percent year-on-year rate. This compared with 3.3 percent month-on-month in December 1996.
Local media quoted Yugoslav Prime Minister Radoje Kontic as saying in an interview that May would bring disinflation.
"It will be an excellent result, bringing inflation in our country in line with that in countries with developed market economies," the state news agency Tanjug quoted Kontic as saying.

But Slobodan Milosavljevic of the IZIT Market Research Institute said even if this proved correct, a fall in prices would be short-lived. "Any deflation would be a consequence of administrative measures, not of real market developments," Milosavljevic said.
Economists said monthly inflation of below two percent would be satisfactory and up to one percent would be a success.

"This would correspond to an annual 20-25 percent inflation and create a satisfactory macro-economic stability for a transition economy to attract domestic savings, foreign investment, more consumer spending," Petrovic said.

While politicians boast about price and currency stability achieved over the last five months, the economists cautioned the rosy picture of macro-economic stability was hiding huge structural imbalances.
Yugoslavia runs a fiscal deficit of four percent of gross domestic product (GDP) and a balance of payments deficit equalling eight percent, Petrovic said.
Yugoslavia covered its external imbalances in 1996 by attracting short-term "hot" capital from abroad, but Petrovic insisted it needed a more reliable source to plug its gaps.
Instead of attracting hot money on high dinar interest rates, economists suggested Yugoslavia should try to woo direct and portfolio investment with more reforms.

Petrovic insisted Yugoslavia's fiscal gap was not extremely high but the problem was how to fund it. "As long as the state finds no healthy source of financing its fiscal imbalances, there is always a threat that it would resort to the mint," he said.
He saw the balance of payments deficit as unavoidable for the country in need of cash to stimulate its idling industries.

But the central bank has been forced to keep tight control over M1 money supply since early January when the dinar reacted to a late-December monetary expansion. This pushed the dinar black market rate down to 4.3 to the German mark, the lowest since 1994.
Although a reduction in M1 during the first quarter helped restore dinar stability and returned the currency to 3.5 to the mark, it has begun to choke production.
Seasonally-adjusted data show first quarter production was three percent down on the last three months of 1996.

By insisting on price and currency stability as its key economic goals for 1997, and on a reduction in prices, the government would need to tighten M1 further. "But that would lead to a recession," Petrovic said.
